candidates.why: Line 1849 assigns str = bit_embed_TU(...), which can return NULL (bit_embed_TU returns NULL at 1804 when wstr is NULL, and bit_embed_TU_size returns NULL at 1578 on malloc failure). Line 1850 then does strlen((const char*)str) with no NULL check before the free at 1854. Not a classic UAF but a NULL-deref on the same object that is later freed; worth flagging as the same lifetime chain.

Line 1874 mallocs ws, line 1875 aliases orig = ws, then the loop advances ws (1884/1888/1891) and writes *ws = 0 at 1893. Line 1894 passes orig to bit_write_TU, which reads chain[i] up to bit_wcs2len(chain)+1 (2144/2150). If the '\U+xxxx' expansion path at 1884-1885 writes more wchars than the (strlen(s)+1)*2 allocation accounts for, the terminator at 1893 and the read at 2150 can run past the buffer that is freed at 1895. Suspicious heap over-read on the object freed at 1895.

Line 2643 utf8 = bit_convert_TU(wstr) may return NULL (2244/2285). Line 2644 guards with 'utf8 ? ... : 0' so the strcmp is safe, but the result is then freed at 2645 unconditionally — free(NULL) is fine, so this is only a low-confidence note that the same pointer is used at 2644 and freed at 2645 with no re-check.

bit_chain_free frees dat->chain at 3032 and sets it NULL at 3033, but does NOT reset dat->num or dat->byte. Any caller that keeps using dat->chain / dat->byte / dat->num after bit_chain_free (e.g. bit_print at 3045-3047 reads dat->size and dat->chain) would be a use-after-free. The free itself is clean; the risk is in callers not shown here, so low confidence.

Not a heap free, but a lifetime/out-of-bounds issue on the same buffer: the loop at 904-906 can exit with i==4 (all byte[0..3] have no 0x7f bits), then line 908 reads byte[i] i.e. byte[4], and line 910 writes byte[i] &= 0x7f. byte[4] is valid (size 5) so this is in-bounds, but the subsequent loop at 913 writes byte[4] down to byte[i]; if i was decremented at 909 the sign bit handling at 911-912 can corrupt the top byte. Flagging as suspicious buffer-index handling adjacent to the write path.

Same pattern as bit_write_MC: loop 975-977 can leave i==4, then 979 reads byte[i] and 981 writes byte[i] &= 0x7f. Additionally 'negative' is declared at 962 but never initialized or used, and byte[5] at 963 is uninitialized (unlike bit_write_MC's zero-init at 889), so if the loop at 969-974 does not fully populate it the read at 979/981 uses indeterminate stack data. Suspicious uninitialized/out-of-range buffer use.
